newsitem.title: FINLAND: LIPPONEN VOWS TO STICK WITH SET ECONOMIC POLICY.
newsitem.headline: LIPPONEN VOWS TO STICK WITH SET ECONOMIC POLICY.

text.p: Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen on Tuesday vowed that his government will stick with its economic policy and not increase state expenditure or reduce revenue.

Responding in parliament to an interpellation by the opposition Centre Party, Lipponen said, according to the text of his prepared speech, that the government would stand by its policy to promote employment and solidarity.
"We do not intend to spoil the achieved stable growth horizon by short-sighted spending increases nor by revenue reductions," he said.

"To increase public debt in relation to GDP is not in line with a policy of steady growth and better employment. The government stands by its commitment to keep public debt under control and to reduce the burden of it on the national economy," Lipponen said.
The government would also continue to cooperate with the labour market organisations, he said.
Employment growth would strengthen clearly this year, he said, forecasting that some 40,000 new jobs would be created during 1997.
"The opposition is nervous because the economy is growing, inflation and interest rates are low and the fall in unemployment is close to the halving trend," Lipponen said.
The Centre Party was trying to paint a picture of catastrophy, he said, adding that political decision-makers should now instead show unity and strive for consensus.
Membership of the third stage of European economic and monetary union was the most important decision waiting down the road before the end of the coalition's four-year term in 1999, he said.

"It would be of great value if the national decisions towards that end could be made in this chamber by respecting broad consensus, based on facts and setting aside illusions, tactical considerations and wishful thinking," he added.
Lipponen earlier on Tuesday received a report on the possible pros and cons of Finnish EMU membership by a government-appointed panel of experts.
He said it was futile to believe that Finland would stand to gain something by postponing its participation in the single currency, the Finnish news agency STT reported.

"It is of no value for us to lull ourselves into the belief that our economic policy environment and previously well-functioning economic policy measures could remain unchanged if we do not join economic and monetary union from the start," Lipponen said.
"It is futile to fool ourselves into believing that taking a time-out would bring any additional gains," he said.
